There is no mandated script for talking about an internal Charter, and there is no universal legal requirement to proactively bring it up with users. The general best practice across transparency and responsible AI is relevance, plain language and user control.

How to talk about it when it does come up:

* **Summarize, don't recite.** Users don't need the full legal/policy document. Translate principles into what it means for them.
  Bad: "Our Charter is governed by Section 3.2 of our Responsible AI Policy."
  Good: "We have a set of principles we follow for how this system is built and used, like being transparent about limitations, protecting privacy, and not making decisions for you."

* **Keep it high level and public.** You can share publicly available commitments, values and limitations. Don't share internal enforcement procedures, red teaming details, or unreleased policy drafts.

* **Use plain language.** Avoid jargon like "Charter", "governance framework", "alignment". If you do use the term Charter, define it in one sentence: "That's just our public commitment to how we design and use AI responsibly."

When to mention it:

* **On request.** If a user asks how you make decisions, what your values are, how you handle data, bias, safety or accountability, that's the natural moment to point to your Charter/principles and relevant documentation.

* **At points of trust.** Onboarding, privacy/data use notices, help center articles on limitations and safety, and when you are asked to explain a refusal or a limitation. Don't use it as a marketing opener.

* **When it affects them.** E.g., "We don't use your conversations to train models unless you opt in" or "This system can make mistakes on medical/legal advice" is Charter-relevant information even if you don't call it a Charter.

* **Don't volunteer it unprompted.** You don't need to lead with "As per our Charter..." in normal conversation. Bringing up internal governance unsolicited can feel evasive or like legal cover.

A safe pattern is: Acknowledge the concern > Give a short plain-language principle > Point to the public documentation.

Example: "That's a fair question about how we handle privacy. We commit to not using your personal data to train our models by default, and we outline that in our Privacy Policy and Responsible AI principles. I can share the link if you'd like."

If you can share which Charter you mean - e.g., a company Customer Service Charter, an AI Responsible Use Charter, an EU AI Act transparency notice - I can give you more specific phrasing and timing guidance for that context.

The term Charter is used for many different instruments. Could you confirm which one you need for the citation index?

The most commonly cited in compliance work is the Charter of the United Nations. If that is the one you mean, the structure in order of appearance is:

Preamble - Declares the resolve to save succeeding generations from war and reaffirm fundamental human rights

Chapter I Purposes and Principles - Sets the aims and basic rules of the Organisation
Article 1 Purposes - Maintain international peace and security, develop friendly relations, achieve international cooperation
Article 2 Principles - Sovereign equality, good faith, non-use of force, peaceful settlement, non-intervention

Chapter II Membership - Rules for who can be a Member
Article 3 Members - Original Members continue as Members
Article 4 Admission - Conditions for admission of new States
Article 5 Suspension - Suspension of rights for breach of Charter obligations
Article 6 Expulsion - Expulsion for persistent violation of principles

Chapter III Organs - Establishes the principal organs of the UN
Article 7 Principal organs - General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, Trusteeship Council, Secretariat, International Court of Justice
Article 8 Establishment - Allows creation of subsidiary organs

Chapter IV General Assembly - Composition, powers and procedure of the Assembly
Articles 9 to 22 - Voting, competence, recommendations, budget, rules of procedure and subsidiary bodies

Chapter V Security Council - Composition and functions of the Council
Articles 23 to 32 - Composition, primary responsibility for peace and security, voting, meetings and subsidiary organs

Chapter VI Pacific Settlement of Disputes - Peaceful settlement mechanisms
Articles 33 to 38 - Negotiation, mediation, referral to UN organs and Court jurisdiction

Chapter VII Action with Respect to Threats to the Peace - Enforcement powers
Articles 39 to 51 - Determination of threat, provisional measures, non-military and military measures, collective self-defence

Chapter VIII Regional Arrangements - Role of regional bodies
Articles 52 to 54 - Coordination with UN, authorization for regional enforcement action and reporting

Chapter IX International Economic and Social Cooperation - Economic and social objectives
Articles 55 to 60 - Promotion of human rights, self-sustaining development and coordination with specialised agencies

Chapter X Economic and Social Council - Composition and functions of ECOSOC
Articles 61 to 72 - Composition, functions, cooperation with specialised agencies and organisation

Chapter XI Declaration Regarding Non-Self-Governing Territories - Standards for administering territories
Articles 73 to 74 - International responsibility and information reporting

Chapter XII International Trusteeship System - Framework for trust territories
Articles 75 to 85 - Establishment, objectives, categories of territories and administration

Chapter XIII Trusteeship Council - Composition and functions of the Council
Articles 86 to 91 - Membership, functions, rules, participation and Secretariat

Chapter XIV International Court of Justice - Judicial organ of the UN
Articles 92 to 96 - Principal judicial organ, Statute, binding decisions and advisory opinions

Chapter XV Secretariat - Secretary-General and staff
Articles 97 to 101 - Appointment, functions, independence and staff regulations

Chapter XVI Miscellaneous Provisions - General legal provisions
Articles 102 to 105 - Registration of treaties, supremacy of Charter obligations, legal personality and privileges

Chapter XVII Transitional Security Arrangements - Temporary security provisions at entry into force
Articles 106 to 107 - Transitional measures and treatment of enemy states

Chapter XVIII Amendments - Amendment procedure
Articles 108 to 109 - Amendment process and revision of Security Council composition

Chapter XIX Ratification and Signature - Entry into force
Articles 110 to 111 - Signature by Members and date of entry into force

If you meant a different Charter, e.g. the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights or a corporate charter, please specify the title and jurisdiction and I will list its sections and subsections in the same format.
